document.title: Les Flaques de Boue - one-minute example

line.source: Il ne pleut plus maintenant. Est-ce qu'on peut sortir jouer ?
line.translation: It isn't raining any more now. Can we go outside and play?
notes: `Est-ce que` introduces a yes/no question without reversing subject and verb. It becomes `est-ce qu'` before `on`; English instead puts can before we.
`On peut sortir jouer` chains two infinitives: we can go out to play. `Sortir` follows `peut`, and `jouer` states the purpose of going out; English supplies and in this translation.

links.note: `Pleut → pleuvoir` = rain, third-person singular present indicative. Weather `il` is impersonal: it does not name a person. `Ne … plus` makes the rain something that has stopped: not any more/no longer.
`Maintenant` = now.

`Peut → pouvoir` = can/be allowed to, third-person singular present indicative with `on`. Here `on` means we, the children asking permission. `Est-ce que` marks the question; `est → être` is third-person singular present indicative inside that fixed question formula.
`Sortir` = go out, an infinitive after `peut`; here it means going outside.
`Jouer` = play, an infinitive expressing what they want to go out to do. English adds and to connect go outside and play.

line.source: Bien sûr. Allez-y et amusez-vous bien.
line.translation: Of course. Go ahead and have fun.
notes: Both commands address the children together. In affirmative commands, the pronouns follow the verb with a hyphen: `allez-y`, `amusez-vous`.

links.note: `Bien sûr` is the fixed expression of course; here it grants permission.
`Allez → aller` = go, second-person plural imperative addressing the children. `Allez-y` means go ahead here; `y` points to going out/the proposed activity.
`Et` = and, joining the two commands.

`Amusez-vous → s'amuser` = have fun/enjoy yourselves, second-person plural imperative. `Amuser quelqu'un` means entertain someone; pronominal `s'amuser` means have fun oneself. `Bien` wishes them a good time.

line.source: Peppa adore sauter dans les flaques de boue.
line.translation: Peppa loves jumping in muddy puddles.
notes: `Adorer + infinitive` names an activity someone loves. French uses the infinitive `sauter`, where this English translation uses jumping.

links.note: `Adore → adorer` = love/really like here, third-person singular present indicative with `Peppa`. It expresses enjoyment rather than worship.
`Sauter` = jump, an infinitive after `adore`; English renders the activity as jumping.
`Dans` = in/into; `une flaque` = a puddle and `la boue` = mud. `Les flaques de boue` literally means the puddles of mud; English naturally says muddy puddles without the article here.

line.source: J'adore sauter dans les flaques de boue.
line.translation: I love jumping in muddy puddles.
notes: `J'adore` expresses Peppa's own enthusiasm. French uses an infinitive for the enjoyed activity: `adorer sauter` = love jumping.

links.note: `Adore → adorer` = love/really like, first-person singular present indicative with `je`, shortened to `j'` before the vowel.
`Sauter` = jump, an infinitive after `adore`, translated here as jumping.
`Dans les flaques de boue` = in muddy puddles: `dans` = in/into, `une flaque` = a puddle and `la boue` = mud. French uses a noun with `de` where English uses the adjective muddy.

line.source: Si tu as envie de sauter dans les flaques, tu dois mettre tes bottes en caoutchouc.
line.translation: If you want to jump in the puddles, you must put on your rubber boots.
notes: `Si` introduces the condition; the second clause states the requirement if that condition applies. Both `as` and `dois` are present indicative.
`Mettre` changes meaning with its object: with clothes, `mettre ses bottes` means put on one’s boots, rather than simply put them somewhere.

links.note: `Si` = if, introducing the condition.

`As → avoir` = have, second-person singular present indicative with `tu`. `Avoir envie de + infinitive` means want to/feel like doing something; `envie` expresses desire here, not jealousy. English puts the desire directly into want.
`Sauter` = jump, an infinitive after `avoir envie de`; it names the desired activity.
`Dans` = in/into; `les flaques` = the puddles, plural of `une flaque`.
`Dois → devoir` = must/have to, second-person singular present indicative with `tu`. It introduces the required action, expressed by the following infinitive.
`Mettre` = put on here, an infinitive after `dois`. Its object is clothing: the boots.
`Tes bottes en caoutchouc` = your rubber boots: `une botte` = a boot, `tes` = your before a plural noun, and `le caoutchouc` = rubber. `En` introduces the material, which English places before boots.
`D'accord` = okay/agreed, accepting the instruction.
`Maman` is a familiar way to address one’s mother, like Mummy or Mum.

line.source: George aussi aime bien sauter dans les flaques de boue.
line.translation: George likes jumping in muddy puddles too.
notes: `Aussi` includes George alongside someone else: George too. French puts it after his name here; this English translation places too at the end. George remains the subject of `aime`.

links.note: `George` names the person who enjoys the activity.
`Aussi` = too/as well here, adding George to the people who like it.
`Aime → aimer` = like, third-person singular present indicative with `George`. `Aimer bien` commonly means like/enjoy; `bien` does not literally mean that he loves well.
`Sauter` = jump, an infinitive naming the activity after `aime bien`; English uses jumping.
`Dans les flaques de boue` = in muddy puddles: `dans` = in/into, `une flaque` = a puddle, and `la boue` = mud. `De boue` describes the kind of puddle.

line.source: George, si tu as envie de sauter dans les flaques de boue, tu dois mettre tes bottes en caoutchouc.
line.translation: George, if you want to jump in muddy puddles, you must put on your rubber boots.
notes: `George` is a direct address. The subject of both clauses is `tu`, meaning the person being addressed: George.
`Si` sets the condition for the requirement in `tu dois`. The desire and obligation both use present indicative forms, `as` and `dois`.

links.note: `George` names the person being addressed.
`Si` = if, opening the condition.

`As → avoir` = have, second-person singular present indicative with `tu`. `Avoir envie de + infinitive` means want to/feel like doing something; `envie` expresses desire here, not jealousy. English puts the desire directly into want.
`Sauter` = jump, an infinitive after `avoir envie de`; it names the activity George wants to do.
`Dans les flaques de boue` = in muddy puddles: `dans` = in/into, `une flaque` = a puddle and `la boue` = mud. English uses muddy for the description `de boue`.
`Dois → devoir` = must/have to, second-person singular present indicative with `tu`. It introduces the required action, expressed by the following infinitive.
`Mettre` = put on with clothing, an infinitive after `dois`. George is the person who must put the boots on.
`Tes bottes en caoutchouc` = your rubber boots: `une botte` = a boot, `tes` = your before a plural noun, and `le caoutchouc` = rubber. `En` introduces the material, which English places before boots.

line.source: Peppa aime bien s'occuper de son petit frère George.
line.translation: Peppa likes looking after her little brother George.
notes: `Son` agrees with the thing or person possessed, masculine singular `frère`, rather than the gender of the possessor. Here it means her because the brother is Peppa’s; the same form can mean his in another context.

links.note: `Aime → aimer` = like/enjoy, third-person singular present indicative with `Peppa`. `Aimer bien` expresses enjoyment here and introduces an infinitive naming the activity.

`S'occuper de quelqu'un` = look after/take care of someone. `Occuper` alone can mean occupy or keep someone busy; the pronominal construction with `de` has this caring meaning. `S'occuper` is an infinitive after `aime bien`; `se` becomes `s'` before the vowel.
`Son petit frère George` = her little brother George. `Un frère` = a brother and `petit frère` means younger/little brother; `son` identifies whose brother he is.
